Energy harvesting

Collection of ambient light, heat flow, thermal cycling, motion or other available energy into a usable electrical supply. Available average power, conversion loss and peak-load buffering must be distinguished.

Conversion of mechanical motion or deformation into electrical energy.

Piezoelectric energy harvesting

Mechanical energy harvesting OurBigBook.com
Electrical generation from mechanically induced electric polarization in a piezoelectric element.

Piezoelectric polymer

Words: 39
Piezoelectric energy harvesting OurBigBook.com
A polymer exhibiting piezoelectricity. A compliant, low-density film can accept larger bending or strain than a brittle ceramic, while low permittivity can yield a large voltage coefficient despite a modest charge coefficient. Extractable energy still depends on mechanical input, capacitance and electrical loading.

Piezoelectric ceramic

Words: 41
Piezoelectric energy harvesting OurBigBook.com
A ceramic material used for piezoelectricity, often offering large charge response and electromechanical coupling with comparatively high stiffness. Brittle fracture, mechanical impedance matching and mounting conditions can limit a vibration harvester. A high charge coefficient alone is not a device power ranking.

Q value (Q=Erest,i​−Erest,f​)

Words: 44
Energy OurBigBook.com
The Q value of a reaction or particle decay is the initial total rest energy minus the final total rest energy. Positive Q releases kinetic energy; a negative Q requires energy supplied by incident motion or another source. Atomic and bare nuclear mass conventions must be distinguished when counting electrons in beta decay.

For a Lagrangian L(q,q˙​,t), its energy function is
E=∑i​q˙​i​∂q˙​i​∂L​−L.

It is conserved along Euler-Lagrange trajectories when L has no explicit time dependence.

Mechanical energy (E=T+V)

Words: 76 Articles: 1
Energy OurBigBook.com
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy. It is conserved when all forces are conservative and the potential has no explicit time dependence.

Conservation of mechanical energy (T+V=constant)

Words: 52
Mechanical energy OurBigBook.com
For constant masses, a time-independent potential energy V and forces Fi​=−∇i​V+Ri​ with zero total extra power ∑i​Ri​⋅vi​=0, Newton's second law gives dT/dt=−dV/dt. Thus mechanical energy is conserved. Smooth stationary constraint reactions and a purely magnetic Lorentz force supply zero power. This is more restrictive than conservation of energy in general, which may include thermal or other internal forms.

Work (W=∫C​F⋅dr)

Words: 834 Articles: 7
Energy OurBigBook.com
Work measures the energy transferred by a force as its point of application moves. For a point mass following a path C, add the contribution of the force along each small displacement:
W=∫C​F⋅dr=∫ti​tf​​F(t)⋅v(t)dt.
(2)
This line integral uses the actual path, and the dot product selects the component of force along the motion. A large force perpendicular to every small displacement does zero work; holding something still also does zero mechanical work on it, even if holding it feels tiring. The SI unit is J=Nm. [ref]
The usefulness of work is that it connects a description in terms of forces and distances to one in terms of energy. The work-energy theorem gives the change in kinetic energy from the total net work, often without solving for the entire motion. The work of one selected force equals that change only when the other forces contribute zero total work.

Work done by a constant force (W=Fdcosθ)

Words: 170
Work OurBigBook.com
For a fixed force F and endpoint displacement Δr, the line integral reduces to a dot product:
W=F⋅Δr=Fdcosθ,F=∣F∣,d=∣Δr∣.
(3)
Here θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. For straight motion, d is also the distance traveled. A 3N force acting along a 4m displacement does 12J of work. Turning the same force perpendicular to the displacement gives cos(π/2)=0 and zero work; reversing it gives cosπ=−1 and −12J. At θ=π/3, the work is 6J. These signs describe energy transferred to or from the moving body. [ref]

Work-energy theorem (Wnet​=ΔT)

Words: 238
Work OurBigBook.com
For a point mass of constant mass m observed in an inertial frame, the net work along its actual path equals its change in kinetic energy:
Wnet​=∫ta​tb​​Fnet​(t)⋅v(t)dt=∫ab​Fnet​⋅dr=21​m∣vb​∣2−21​m∣va​∣2.
(4)
The middle expression is a line integral; the dot product selects the component of force along the displacement. Positive net work increases speed, negative net work decreases it, and zero net work leaves the endpoint speeds equal. Equal endpoint speeds do not imply equal velocities: a perpendicular force can continually change direction while doing zero work. [ref]
The bridge to Newton's second law is short: take the dot product of mv˙=Fnet​ with velocity. The chain rule gives d(m∣v∣2/2)/dt=Fnet​⋅v, equating the rate of change of kinetic energy to instantaneous power. Integrating gives the theorem. No conservative force assumption entered this argument; friction also contributes to the net work.
For the harmonic oscillator with spring stiffness k=2N/m, release a mass m=0.5kg from rest at x=0.3m. The spring exerts F=−kx. Its work before the first passage through x=0 is
W=∫0.3m0​(−kx)dx=21​k(0.3m)2=0.09J.
(5)
Thus mv2/2=0.09J gives speed 0.6m/s there. The velocity is negative on this passage because the position is decreasing. The energy calculation alone determines its magnitude, so the direction still requires information about the motion.
For a time-independent potential energy V, the conservative force contributes work −ΔV. Separating all other work as Wother​ gives Δ(T+V)=Wother​. Consequently conservation of mechanical energy requires zero net other work; the work-energy theorem itself does not require that conservation. With damping, mechanical energy decreases even though the theorem remains valid. [ref]

Power (P=dW/dt)

Words: 290 Articles: 4
Work OurBigBook.com
Power describes how quickly energy is transferred. For mechanical work, the instantaneous power supplied by a force is
P(t)=dtdW​=F(t)⋅v(t),W=∫ti​tf​​P(t)dt.
(6)
The SI unit is W=J/s=Nm/s, distinct from the velocity unit m/s. The italic symbol W for work and the upright unit W for power mean different things. Two processes can transfer the same energy while requiring different powers: doing 12J of work in 2s requires an average 6W, whereas doing it in 4s requires an average 3W. [ref]

Power OurBigBook.com
Power output or input divided by the relevant mass, commonly expressed in watts per kilogram. Device-level and active-material values cannot be compared without stating their different mass bases.

Peak power (Ppk​)

Words: 7
Power OurBigBook.com
The maximum instantaneous power in a specified pulse.

Instantaneous power (P(t)=F(t)⋅v(t))

Words: 75
Power OurBigBook.com
Instantaneous power is power at a particular moment. Consider a point mass with mass m=2kg, initially at rest, acted on by a constant net force F=3N along a straight path. Newton's second law gives constant acceleration a=F/m=1.5m/s2, hence velocity v(t)=at and
P(t)=Fat=(4.5W/s)t.
(7)
The instantaneous power starts at zero even though the force is nonzero, because the initial velocity is zero. At distance 4m, the kinetic energy example below gives speed 12​m/s, so the final instantaneous power is 312​W≈10.3923W. Negative instantaneous power means the selected force is removing energy at that moment.

Average power (P=W/(tf​−ti​))

Words: 93
Power OurBigBook.com
Average power divides the work over a nonzero interval by the elapsed time. For the same 2kg point mass driven from rest through 4m by a net 3N force, the displacement is x(t)=at2/2. Thus
tf​=1.5m/s22(4m)​​=16/3​s≈2.309401s,P=tf​12J​≈5.19615W.
(8)
This average power is half the final instantaneous power because P(t) is a linear function of time, starting at zero. Its graph of a function bounds a triangle of area P(tf​)tf​/2=12J; the horizontal line at average power encloses a rectangle with the same area. In general, an endpoint value of instantaneous power does not determine average power. [ref]

Kinetic energy (K=21​mv2)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Energy OurBigBook.com
Kinetic energy is the energy associated with motion. For a nonrelativistic point mass of mass m>0, measured in a specified inertial frame,
K=21​mv⋅v=21​mv2,v=∣v∣.
(9)
Here v is velocity and v is speed; T is another common symbol for kinetic energy. The dot product makes K nonnegative regardless of the direction of velocity. At fixed mass, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy: a 2kg point mass at 2m/s has 4J, whereas at 4m/s it has 16J. The SI units are kgm2/s2=J. Different reference frames can assign different velocities and therefore different kinetic energies. [ref]
A short outline explains why kinetic energy has this formula. In a nonrelativistic inertial frame, constant mass and Newton's second law give, using the chain rule,
dtdK​=mv⋅dtdv​=Fnet​⋅v.
(10)
Integrating over time proves the work-energy theorem, Wnet​=Kf​−Ki​. The net force is the sum of all forces, and Wnet​ is their total work, not merely the work of a chosen driving force. This route to final speed is useful when the forces as functions of position are known but the full motion as a function of time would be harder to find. [ref]
In the running example, a 2kg point mass starts at rest and receives a constant net 3N force through 4m. Its net work is 12J, so
Kf​=12J,vf​=m2Kf​​​=12​m/s≈3.4641m/s.
(11)
At any intermediate distance x≥0, K(x)=(3N)x and v(x)=2Fx/m​: kinetic energy is a linear function of distance, while speed is proportional to the square root of distance. If a net opposing 3N braking force subsequently acts for 4m, it does −12J of work and brings this point mass to rest. Negative net work decreases kinetic energy; it does not make kinetic energy negative. Beyond the stopping point the motion must be reconsidered, since the point mass cannot keep moving forward with a negative K.
Kinetic energy also makes the exchange with potential energy intuitive: a falling body's loss of gravitational potential energy can appear as increased kinetic energy. The formula above applies when speed is small compared with the speed of light; at higher speeds, special relativity changes the expression. [ref]

Kinetic energy correction factor (α=Au3∫A​u3dA​)

Words: 46
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
For unidirectional flow through area A with mean speed u, the outgoing kinetic-energy flux is 21​ρAαu3, where α=(Au3)−1∫A​u3dA. Cubing the mean speed generally differs from averaging the cube. A uniform profile has α=1; circular laminar Hagen-Poiseuille flow has α=2.

Relativistic kinetic energy (K=(γ−1)mc2)

Words: 29
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
For a free particle of rest mass m, subtract its rest energy mc2 from its total energy γmc2, where γ is the Lorentz factor. The low-speed binomial series gives K=mv2/2+3mv4/(8c2)+O(mv6/c4), recovering classical kinetic energy.

Rigid rotation minimizes kinetic energy at fixed angular momentum (K≥L2/(2I))

Words: 136
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
For rotational motion about a fixed axis, let r be cylindrical radius, v the signed tangential velocity, and dm the mass measure. Define the kinetic energy, axial angular momentum, and moment of inertia by
K=21​∫v2dm,L=∫rvdm,I=∫r2dm>0.
(12)
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives L2≤(∫v2dm)(∫r2dm)=2KI. More precisely, direct expansion gives the nonnegative energy gap
K−2IL2​=21​∫(v−IL​r)2dm.
(13)
Thus the minimum at fixed L and fixed mass distribution occurs exactly when v=(L/I)r almost everywhere with respect to dm. This means constant angular velocity Ω=L/I, or solid-body rotation. If the profile is continuous, the equality holds at every point in the mass support.
For a uniform unit-density cylinder of radius a, height h, and volume V=πa2h, the moment of inertia is I=Va2/2. Therefore K≥L2/(Va2), with equality for ω(r)=2L/(Va2). Multiplying by a uniform nonunit density changes the mass measure and I consistently.

Kinetic energy decomposition about the center of mass (T=21​M∣R˙∣2+21​∑i​mi​∣ρ˙​i​∣2)

Words: 52
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
Writing particle positions relative to the center of mass as ρi​=ri​−R makes ∑i​mi​ρi​=0, so the cross term in the squared velocities vanishes. The total kinetic energy splits into center-of-mass translation and relative motion as displayed. For a rigid body, the latter is 21​Iω2, where I is the moment of inertia about the instantaneous rotation axis through the center of mass.

Unit-direction kinetic-energy identity (v2=(u⋅v)2−r2u⋅u¨)

Words: 52
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
For a twice differentiable position away from the origin, write r=ru with radial unit vector u. Its unit-length constraint gives u⋅u˙=0 and u⋅u¨=−∣u˙∣2, separating radial and directional contributions to speed and kinetic energy. The identity is kinematic and does not require a particular force law.

Kinetic energy density

Words: 30
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
The kinetic energy density of a continuum with mass density ρ and velocity v is ρ∣v∣2/2. For a displacement field, the material velocity is its time derivative.

Rotational kinetic energy (K=21​Iω2)

Words: 339
Kinetic energy OurBigBook.com
Rotational kinetic energy is the kinetic energy of a rigid body's rotation. For pure rotation about an axis fixed in an inertial frame,
Krot​=21​Iω2,I=∫r⊥2​dm,ω=∣ω∣.
(14)
Here r⊥​ is the perpendicular distance of a mass element dm from that axis, I is the moment of inertia about that same axis, and ω is the common angular speed, measured in radians per second. The rigid body assumption fixes the relative positions of the mass elements; they share angular velocity but have different speeds v=ωr⊥​. Summing their kinetic energies dmv2/2 gives the formula. This is a nonrelativistic model; deformation or internal motion can contribute additional kinetic energy.[ref]
For a computed example, take a uniform disc and an ideal thin ring, each of mass M=2kg and radius R=0.30m, rotating about its central perpendicular axis at angular speed 10rad/s. The moment of inertia of a uniform disc is MR2/2=0.090kgm2, while the ring has moment of inertia MR2=0.180kgm2. Their rotational kinetic energies are therefore 4.5J and 9.0J. The ring stores twice the energy at the same angular speed, because more mass lies farther from the axis. At the same nonzero rotational kinetic energy, its angular speed would instead be 1/2​ times the disc's. This makes radial placement useful for storing energy in a rotating wheel, although a real design must also withstand the stresses of rotation.
For fixed-axis rotation with constant moment of inertia, write the signed rotation rate as Ω=θ˙, with angle θ in radians. The axial component of net external torque obeys τaxis​=IΩ˙, so the work-energy theorem becomes
dtdKrot​​=τaxis​Ω,ΔKrot​=∫τaxis​dθ.
(15)
An opposing torque removes rotational kinetic energy; bearing friction must be included in the net torque. The signed Ω matters when the direction reverses. Rotation about a fixed axis need not be about a principal axis: the scalar energy formula still holds, but transverse bearing torques can be needed to maintain that axis.
For general rigid body motion, use the inertia tensor IG​ about the centre of mass G:
Ktotal​=21​M∣VG​∣2+21​ωTIG​ω,LG​=IG​ω.
(16)
This is the kinetic-energy decomposition about the centre of mass. In a principal body frame, the rotational term is 21​(I1​ω12​+I2​ω22​+I3​ω32​), using the principal moments of inertia. Away from a principal axis, angular momentum and angular velocity need not be parallel. A freely rotating asymmetric rigid body can change the direction of angular velocity relative to the body even while rotational kinetic energy remains constant; Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body govern that motion. One constant axial moment of inertia is then insufficient.[ref]

Potential energy (F=−∇V)

Words: 3k Articles: 34
Energy OurBigBook.com
Potential energy assigns energy to a system's arrangement, so a change of arrangement accounts for the work done by a conservative force. For a time-independent potential energy V(r),
F=−∇V,Wconservative​=Vi​−Vf​=−ΔV.
(17)
The gradient points toward increasing potential energy; the force points toward decreasing potential energy. Only differences matter: adding a constant to V changes neither the force nor its work. This endpoint rule follows by substituting −∇V into the line integral for work. [ref]
Near Earth's surface, stipulate constant gravitational acceleration g=9.81m/s2 and measure height h upward from a chosen zero. Then gravitational potential energy is V=mgh. Raising a 2kg mass by 0.5m increases its gravitational potential energy by 9.81J, while gravity does −9.81J of work. These are computed model values, not measurements of a particular lift. An ideal spring obeying Hooke's law instead has V=kx2/2, with displacement x from its relaxed state and spring constant k: k=100N/m and x=0.2m give V=2J relative to x=0. [ref]

Lennard-Jones potential (U(r)=4ϵ[(σ/r)12−(σ/r)6])

Words: 58
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
Named after John Lennard-Jones, this is a pair potential energy combining steep short-range repulsion with nonretarded London dispersion force attraction. Its minimum is U=−ϵ at r=21/6σ, found by differentiation. The power twelve is a convenient model for repulsion, rather than an exact consequence of the Pauli exclusion principle. The power six in the attractive energy follows from second-order coupling of atomic electric dipoles, before retardation matters.

Harmonic potential (V(x)=21​kx2)

Words: 48
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
A quadratic potential energy about a stable equilibrium. In one dimension k>0 is the restoring stiffness and the force is −dV/dx=−kx. A mass m undergoing undamped motion has angular frequency k/m​. A smooth potential with a nondegenerate local minimum is approximately harmonic for sufficiently small displacements; higher-order terms describe departures from simple harmonic motion.

Words: 64 Articles: 1
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
A region of lower potential energy surrounded by higher potential energy; a particle must gain sufficient energy to escape classically.

Half-line square-root potential well (V(x)=ax​,x>0,ψ(0)=0)

Words: 48
Potential well OurBigBook.com
A confining Quantum Hamiltonian on x>0 with a>0, potential ax​ and a Dirichlet boundary condition at zero has natural length ℓ=(ℏ2/(2ma))2/5 and energy E∗​=(ℏ2a4/(2m))1/5. Rescaling x=ℓy gives H/E∗​=−d2/dy2+y​, so every energy eigenvalue scales as E∗​. The potential derivative diverges at the wall even though the potential itself is finite there.

Repulsive inverse-square potential (V(r)=c/r2,c>0)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
This potential energy generates a repulsive central force Fr​=−V′(r)=2c/r3. It is an inverse-square potential but an inverse-cube force; the powers must not be confused with the Coulomb or gravitational potential proportional to 1/r.

Scattering in a repulsive inverse-square potential (r=rmin​sec[β(θ−θ0​)])

Words: 59
Repulsive inverse-square potential OurBigBook.com
For V(r)=c/r2 with c>0, nonzero physical angular momentum h and positive energy E, put β=1+2mc/h2​>1 and rmin​=(c+h2/(2m))/E​. Direct integration of the effective potential radial equation gives the displayed orbit. It has one radial minimum and two straight-line asymptotes separated by polar angle π/β. The repulsive scattering deflection is π−π/β; no bounded or circular orbit exists at finite positive energy.

Gravitational energy (Egrav​)

Words: 52
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
The potential energy associated with gravitational interactions. For a self-gravitating spherical body with a fixed dimensionless density profile, Egrav​=−CGM2/R for a positive profile-dependent constant C; a uniform sphere has C=3/5. The R−1 scaling competes with the same radius dependence of ultrarelativistic electron degeneracy pressure in a white dwarf, giving the Chandrasekhar mass scale.

Available potential energy (A)

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
The portion of a fluid system's potential energy that can be released by admissible rearrangement relative to a stable reference state. In a uniformly stratified incompressible fluid, the quadratic density is A=ρ0​N2ξz2​/2=ρ0​b2/(2N2), where ξz​ is vertical fluid displacement and b the buoyancy perturbation. It is positive for stable stratification and measures the restoring energy of internal gravity waves.

Background potential energy (Pb​)

Words: 50
Available potential energy OurBigBook.com
The background potential energy is the gravitational potential energy of the statically stable state obtained by adiabatically sorting a fluid's parcels. The difference A=P−Pb​ is available potential energy. Pure rearrangement changes A but not Pb​; irreversible density mixing can increase Pb​. Molecular exchange with internal energy must be separated when defining an irreversible mixing rate.

A potential function V assigns a scalar to each point of a configuration or spatial domain. In mechanics it represents potential energy, and its negative gradient gives the corresponding conservative force.

A central potential depends only on distance from a fixed centre, V(x)=V(∣x∣). Its force is radial, and rotational symmetry implies conservation of angular momentum.

Adding an inverse-cube force can preserve radial motion while rescaling angular motion. For potential −A/r+B/r2 and angular momentum L, the radial effective potential equals that of −A/r with effective angular momentum L2+2mB​ when this is real.

A force is conservative when its work depends only on the endpoints. On a simply connected domain this is equivalent to F=−∇V for a potential energy V.

Nonconservative force

Conservative force OurBigBook.com
A nonconservative force has path-dependent work. On a simply connected domain, a continuously differentiable force is nonconservative exactly when its curl does not vanish identically.

Inverse-square potential (V(r)=−k/r)

Words: 805 Articles: 5
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
Here inverse-square potential means the potential energy associated with an attractive inverse-square law for a central force: the potential energy itself varies as inverse distance. For k>0 and position r with r=∣r∣>0,
V(r)=−rk​,V(∞)=0,F=−∇V=−r2k​r=−r3kr​.
(18)
The gradient makes the distinction explicit: doubling r halves the magnitude of potential energy but quarters the magnitude of force. The neighboring repulsive inverse-square potential instead has potential energy proportional to r−2 and an inverse-cube force; the two naming conventions must be distinguished.
For Newton's law of universal gravitation, k=GMm, where G is the gravitational constant. Treat the attracting mass M as an isolated fixed point mass, or as a body with spherical symmetry and exterior test particle of constant mass m≪M. The spherical shell theorem gives the same exterior Newtonian gravitational potential energy U=−GMm/r without requiring uniform mass density. Here r is measured from the centre, and the formula applies outside the body; it does not describe its interior. The Newtonian gravitational potential per unit mass is Φ=U/m=−GM/r.[ref]
The negative sign records binding relative to infinite separation, rather than a negative kinetic energy. Moving from r1​ to r2​>r1​ increases potential energy by
ΔV=k(r1​1​−r2​1​)>0,Wgravity​=−ΔV.
(19)
Because the force is a conservative force, this work depends on the endpoints, including for a curved path. Integrating dV/dr=k/r2 with zero at infinity gives V=−k/r; adding a constant leaves the force unchanged but shifts the numerical escape energy threshold by that same constant. This is why the reference at infinity must accompany an escape velocity calculation.
For an exact synthetic comparison, stipulate the standard gravitational parameter μ=GM=8m3/s2 and a 1kg test particle. At r=2m, U=−4J and the inward force has magnitude 2N; at r=4m, U=−2J and the inward force has magnitude 0.5N. The increase is 2J of potential energy. These stipulated parameters are an arithmetic example, not observations of a particular body. The escape-energy balance diagram uses the same parameters.

Angular momentum and the escape energy threshold (ε=21​r˙2+2r2h2​−rμ​)

Words: 150
Inverse-square potential OurBigBook.com
In the isolated model, conservation of energy and angular momentum conservation reduce the exterior test particle's motion to
ε=mE​=2r˙2​+2r2h2​−rμ​,h=∣r×v∣,μ=GM.
(20)
Here ε is specific orbital energy and h is specific angular momentum. The effective potential is Φeff​=h2/(2r2)−μ/r. A zero radial velocity is a radial turning point, and need not mean zero total speed: at the periapsis or apoapsis of a nonradial Kepler orbit, tangential velocity remains. Thus the vertical gap between ε and −μ/r represents total kinetic energy per unit mass, whereas the gap above Φeff​ represents its radial part.
For h>0, the orbital eccentricity obeys e2=1+2εh2/μ2. Negative ε gives an elliptic orbit, including a circular orbit at its minimum allowed energy; zero ε gives a parabolic trajectory; positive ε gives a hyperbolic Kepler orbit. The effective potential tends to zero from below at infinity, so its outer region creates no extra positive escape barrier. This explains why escape velocity depends on energy even though angular momentum changes the path. The h=0 case is radial motion, rather than a nondegenerate parabola or hyperbola; inward radial motion can end in collision.

Falling bodies and lunar motion as tests of gravity

Words: 140
Inverse-square potential OurBigBook.com
One motivating laboratory demonstration compares two balls initially at the same height. A switch releases one vertically when the other leaves a horizontal track; arranging their paths to meet gives a collision as the readout of equal downward displacement over equal time. Equal initial height and synchronized release control the comparison. This tests the local independence of horizontal motion and free fall, under nearly constant gravitational acceleration; it does not measure an inverse-square law.[ref]
A complementary astronomical comparison uses the Moon's distance and orbital period to infer inward centripetal acceleration, a=4π2r/T2, and compares it with surface gravitational acceleration scaled by (R/r)2. The approximately sixtyfold distance ratio gives the approximately 1/3600 prediction. The inference links terrestrial free fall to a lunar orbit. Distance calibration matters; the circular orbit approximation and the Sun's tidal force limit this elementary comparison.[ref]

Lunar laser ranging

Words: 227 Articles: 2
Inverse-square potential OurBigBook.com
Lunar laser ranging gives a more discriminating orbit readout. An observatory directs short laser pulses at a retroreflector array on the Moon, and a detector records returning photons. Round-trip time, statistically combined over several returns, constrains distance; pressure and temperature accompany the readout. The fitted model includes Newtonian gravity, terrestrial and lunar rotation, geophysical effects, and corrections from general relativity. Comparing orbit determination residuals across stations and model choices checks consistency. The inspected study reports 1.8cm weighted root mean square residuals for its 2005–2011 ranges, rather than for a bare isolated inverse-square potential. It tests the equivalence principle using the Earth and Moon's response to the Sun; it is not a direct escape velocity measurement. Uneven coverage near new and full Moon, radiation pressure, and thermal expansion of reflector mounts limit that inference.[ref]
Retroreflector
Words: 97 Articles: 1
Lunar laser ranging OurBigBook.com
A retroreflector returns incident light approximately toward its source. Corner-cube arrays make the lunar laser ranging round trip possible.
Corner reflector
Words: 83
Retroreflector OurBigBook.com
Three mutually perpendicular mirrors reverse a ray's direction when it encounters all three. With orthonormal normals a,b,c, write the reflections as I−2Pa​, I−2Pb​, I−2Pc​. Their orthogonal projection matrices have pairwise products zero and sum to I by the resolution of the identity in an orthonormal basis. The product of the three reflections is therefore −I. It reverses every incident direction independently of the order in which the mirrors are met. Real apertures restrict which incoming rays actually reach all three reflecting faces. Such retroreflectors provide the returning-light geometry in lunar laser ranging.

Exponential cusp potential

Words: 30
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
The even potential
V(x)=V∞​(1−e−∣x∣/λ)
(21)
has a cusp at the origin and approaches the finite value V∞​. Motions below that value oscillate between symmetric turning points; motions above it escape.

Escape velocity (vesc​=2GM/r​)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
The escape velocity is the least initial speed that permits a freely coasting body to move arbitrarily far from an isolated attracting body. Despite its conventional name, it is a speed, not a unique velocity vector. For a fixed point mass M, or outside a body with spherical symmetry, set Newtonian gravitational potential energy zero at infinity. An exterior test particle of constant mass m≪M then has
U(r)=−rGMm​,E=21​mv2−rGMm​,vesc​(r)=r2GM​​=r2μ​​.
(22)
Here μ=GM is the standard gravitational parameter, and r is distance from the centre, not height above the surface. Set r=R for surface escape velocity. Evaluate velocity in the body's rest inertial frame. Neglect drag, later rocket thrust, other bodies' gravity, and relativistic effects.[ref]
Conservation of energy gives the threshold by requiring E≥0: at infinity the potential energy tends to zero and the kinetic energy cannot be negative. If E=0, the outward motion loses speed continuously toward zero. If E>0, the asymptotic speed is v∞​=2E/m​=v02​−vesc​(r0​)2​. If E<0, infinity is inaccessible. For a radial outward launch, its outer turning point is rmax​=−GMm/E. For nonradial motion use angular momentum and the escape energy threshold to distinguish zero radial velocity from zero total speed.
Direction still determines the orbit and whether the body hits an obstacle. An initially inward velocity can cause collision even when E≥0. For an isolated spherical body, an exterior outward launch, or a tangential launch at or above escape velocity, has an outward escape branch without intersecting the body. A parabolic trajectory is the nonradial threshold path; a hyperbolic Kepler orbit has positive energy. The formula specifies their required local speed, not their orientation.[ref]

Escape by jumping from a uniform-density asteroid (rmax​=RH​)

Words: 75
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
For a spherical nonrotating asteroid of the same mean mass density as a reference planet of radius R and surface gravity g, the mass scales as r cubed. Its surface escape speed therefore obeys vesc2​=2gr2/R. A take-off speed vJ​ permits escape for r≤vJ​R/(2g)​. If that same take-off speed gives ballistic height H above the reference planet, vJ2​=2gH, and the limiting asteroid radius is RH​. A chosen H is an explicit performance estimate, not a universal human constant.

Molecular escape-speed temperature estimate

Words: 37
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
Equating the molecular root-mean-square speed to the surface escape velocity gives 3kB​T/m=2GM/R, or T=2mGM/(3kB​R). This compares speed scales; the high-speed tail can escape below that temperature, and molecular dissociation can invalidate the assumed species at high temperature.

Escape-energy balance diagram

Words: 140
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
Use the synthetic standard gravitational parameter μ=8m3/s2 and launch distance r0​=2m. Then escape speed is 22​m/s. Three outward radial launches give exact comparisons: v0​=2m/s has specific orbital energy −2J/kg and stops outward at r=4m; v0​=22​m/s has zero specific orbital energy; v0​=23​m/s has specific orbital energy +2J/kg and asymptotic speed 2m/s. The second case has speed 2m/s at r=4m. Doubling r0​ divides escape speed by 2​, whereas doubling M at fixed r0​ multiplies it by 2​. Changing the test particle's mass changes E but cancels from the escape speed.

Tangential launch trajectories across the escape threshold (r=1+ecosfh2/μ​)

Words: 192
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
The same initial distance can lead to strikingly different orbits. Let s=v0​/μ/r0​​≥1 and launch tangentially in one orbital plane. Then periapsis is the launch point, specific angular momentum is h=r0​v0​, and
μ/r0​ε​=2s2​−1,e=s2−1,r0​r​=1+(s2−1)cosfs2​,
(23)
where f is true anomaly. These follow by combining the initial specific orbital energy with the orbital eccentricity relation and the Kepler orbit equation. With μ=8m3/s2 and r0​=2m, the initial speeds 2, 6​, 22​, and 23​m/s give e=0,1/2,1,2: a circular orbit, an elliptic orbit with apoapsis distance 6m, a parabolic trajectory, and a hyperbolic Kepler orbit. The two open paths have asymptotic speeds zero and 2m/s respectively. Their different directions at large distance are part of the Kepler orbit, not an extra scalar escape threshold.

Zero-energy escape takes infinite time (r(t)=[r03/2​+23​2μ​t]2/3)

Words: 92
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
“Arrives at infinity with zero speed” is an asymptotic statement. For outward radial motion at zero specific orbital energy,
r˙=r2μ​​,t(r)=32μ​2​(r3/2−r03/2​),r(t)=(r03/2​+23​2μ​t)2/3.
(24)
Every finite distance takes finite time, but t(r)→∞ as r→∞. There is no instant of rest at an infinitely distant destination. Differentiating the displayed solution gives r¨=−μ/r2, independently checking Newton's second law. In the synthetic example, reaching r=4m takes exactly (4−2​)/3s≈0.861929s. For nonzero specific angular momentum, the Barker equation gives the corresponding infinite-time limit along a parabolic trajectory. Positive-energy escape also takes infinite time to reach infinity; it retains nonzero asymptotic speed.

Escape speed, circular speed, and propulsion

Words: 213
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
For a circular orbit, gravity supplies centripetal acceleration, giving vc2​/r=μ/r2. Thus
vc​=rμ​​,vesc​=2​vc​,εc​=−2rμ​.
(25)
A body in a circular orbit is bound despite its continuous free fall. At the same r, escape needs twice its kinetic energy per unit mass. An instantaneous forward tangential velocity increment from the circular orbit requires Δv=(2​−1)vc​, rather than the full escape speed from rest. In the synthetic example this is exactly 2(2​−1)m/s≈0.828427m/s.[ref]
Escape speed is a coasting threshold, not a required continuously maintained speed or a measure of rocket propellant. A powered vehicle can start at rest and acquire energy gradually. The rocket equation relates an ideal velocity increment to rocket exhaust speed and rocket mass ratio; rocket thrust, drag, and the timing and direction of propulsion affect a real ascent. Rotation also changes the relation between surface-relative velocity and the inertial frame used in the calculation.
Reaching another body is a finite-destination spacecraft trajectory problem. In the synthetic radial example, a launch at 2m/s reaches r=4m while remaining bound. A spacecraft can similarly encounter the Moon on a bound geocentric transfer; actual planning must include the Moon's gravity, target motion, arrival velocity, and any propulsion needed for capture. Escaping Earth alone does not imply escaping the Sun, because the relevant reference frame and attracting mass have changed. The isolated formula describes one gravitational well; a full mission requires more than its scalar threshold.

Spacecraft tracking and the limits of the escape model

Words: 131
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
Operational evidence comes from reconstructing a spacecraft's motion. A ground antenna transmits a coded signal; the spacecraft returns it. Corrected round-trip time constrains distance, while the Doppler effect of a coherent carrier constrains the line-of-sight relative velocity. NASA's navigation account describes calibration of onboard turnaround delays before launch, calibration of ground delays before use, and corrections for the terrestrial atmosphere. Measurements over multiple stations and epochs constrain the orbit; range and Doppler effect alone do not directly give all transverse motion. Navigators compare a fitted spacecraft trajectory with later tracking and remeasure after propulsion to assess the maneuver. The account identifies radiation pressure and imperfect propulsion as disturbances. This provides practical checks of a dynamical model and its corrections, rather than a laboratory measurement of a universal escape speed. The simple inverse-square potential predicts an unpowered exterior arc; accurate navigation includes additional forces and measurement delays.[ref]

Spacecraft trajectory

Words: 49 Articles: 1
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
A spacecraft trajectory is the path traced by a spacecraft's position over time. An unpowered exterior arc can approximate a Kepler orbit; other bodies' gravity, radiation pressure, and propulsion can change it.
Orbit determination
Words: 22
Spacecraft trajectory OurBigBook.com
Orbit determination infers a body's position and velocity from observations and an equation of motion. It is an inverse problem; a residual of an inverse problem compares an observed readout with its modeled prediction.

Escape and circular speeds inside an isolated uniform sphere (ve2​=Vc2​(3r02​/r2−1))

Words: 66
Escape velocity OurBigBook.com
For a sphere of radius r0​ and uniform mass density ρ0​, with no surrounding mass and gravitational potential zero at infinity, the spherical shell theorem gives Vc2​=4πGρ0​r2/3 inside. Matching to the exterior point-mass potential gives Φ(r)=−(2πGρ0​/3)(3r02​−r2). Since ve2​=−2Φ, the displayed relation follows for 0<r≤r0​. Exterior shells leave the interior circular speed unchanged but deepen the potential and change the escape velocity; a uniform core alone is insufficient to determine escape.

Equipotential surface

Words: 64 Articles: 1
Potential energy OurBigBook.com
An equipotential surface is a level set of a scalar potential. Its gradient and the corresponding conservative force are normal to every smooth level surface.

Equipotential curve (ϕ(x,y)=C)

Words: 39
Equipotential surface OurBigBook.com
An equipotential curve is a planar level curve of a scalar potential. Where the gradient is nonzero, its tangent is perpendicular to that gradient. In potential flow, it is therefore perpendicular to the velocity field; this distinguishes equipotential curves from streamlines.

Turning point

Words: 23
Energy OurBigBook.com
A turning point of one-dimensional motion is a position where the kinetic energy and instantaneous velocity vanish before the direction of motion reverses.

Binding energy

Words: 26
Energy OurBigBook.com
Binding energy is the energy required to separate a bound state into specified free constituents. For an electron bound in a chemical atom, neglecting this cost is an assumption of the free-electron Compton scattering model.
